lines.t: Evolution is history. And history, normally, happens only once.
Stephen Jay Gould asked what would happen if we could rewind the tape of life and play it again.
In a laboratory, we can. This film is about how it is done, and why each step of the method exists.

scenes.title: Why evolve life in a flask?

lines.t: In nature, we meet evolution after the fact. We see the survivors, never the losers, and never the alternatives.
An evolution experiment turns that history into a controlled experiment. It rests on four ideas.
Control: we choose the ancestor and the environment, so we know exactly what changed.
Replication: many populations start out identical, so we can separate what is repeatable from what is chance.
Time travel: microbes survive freezing, so the past stays alive and can be compared with the present.
And scale: one flask holds billions of cells, and hundreds of generations pass in a few months.
Most microbial evolution experiments follow the same recipe, and each step removes one source of ambiguity.
Start from one clone. Define the environment. Propagate by serial transfer. Freeze samples. Replicate. Measure fitness by competition.
Let's take the steps one at a time, and ask of each: what do we do, and why?
First, the ancestor is streaked thinly across a plate, and a single colony is picked: the descendants of one cell.
Why? Because then every cell in the starting population carries the same genome.
Any genetic difference that appears later must be a new mutation, born during the experiment.
Without this, a variant that rises might have been there from the start, and we could not tell new from old.
The ancestor's genome is sequenced too. It is the reference that every later genome is compared against.
Next, choose the challenge. Here, a defined minimal medium in which glucose runs out before anything else.
Why defined? Every ingredient is known and weighed, so the selective pressure is the same in every flask, every week.
Why limit one nutrient? It makes the currency of competition clear: above all, the cells are racing for glucose.
Temperature, volume, flask shape and shaking speed are fixed as well, because each of them is part of the environment.
Change any of them, and the meaning of fitter changes too. That idea returns at the end.
Now the population grows. Over 48 hours the cells wake up, ferment glucose, switch to respiring ethanol, and finally stop.
lines.say: Now the population grows. Over forty-eight hours the cells wake up, ferment glucose, switch to respiring ethanol, and finally stop.

lines.t: Then a small sample, 400 µL of the 100 mL, is moved into fresh medium, and the cycle repeats.
lines.say: Then a small sample, four hundred microlitres of the hundred millilitres, is moved into fresh medium, and the cycle repeats.

lines.t: Why transfer at all? A closed flask is a dead end. Transfers let evolution run for as long as we like.
Why this dilution? After a 250-fold dilution, the cells must double about eight times to refill the flask: eight generations per cycle.
lines.say: Why this dilution? After a two-hundred-fifty-fold dilution, the cells must double about eight times to refill the flask: eight generations per cycle.

lines.t: And the environment is a cycle of feast and famine, not a constant. Selection acts on every phase: waking quickly, growing fast, switching well.
A chemostat, the main alternative, holds conditions constant instead. Each design asks a slightly different question.
How many cells to transfer is not a detail. It sets the balance between selection and chance.
Every transfer is a random draw. A new mutant that is still a single cell is easily left behind, however good it is.
A mutant with a 5% advantage must reach roughly twenty cells, about one over its advantage, before it is reliably safe from that lottery.
lines.say: A mutant with a five percent advantage must reach roughly twenty cells, about one over its advantage, before it is reliably safe from that lottery.

lines.t: Large transfers also mean a large supply of mutations: the number arising each generation is population size times mutation rate.
With tens of millions of cells per transfer, many good mutations arise and some survive. With a tiny bottleneck, chance would throw most of them away.
At every transfer, the leftover cells are frozen at minus eighty degrees, in a solution that protects them from ice.
Why? The frozen samples are a fossil record that can be revived. Ancestors and descendants can be grown side by side and compared directly.
They also let evolution be replayed from any point, and they are insurance against contamination.
And the experiment is run in replicate: several populations from the same ancestor, in identical conditions.
Why? If independent populations hit the same gene again and again, chance is an unlikely explanation. Parallel evolution is a signature of selection.
Finally, how do we know a population has adapted? We measure fitness, and fitness is always relative.
The evolved strain is mixed with a marked copy of the ancestor in one flask, and their ratio is tracked over several cycles.
Why compete, instead of measuring growth rate? Because selection sees the whole cycle: lag, growth, the switch, and survival. A head-to-head race adds them all up.
Because both grow exponentially, the log of their ratio changes along a straight line. Its slope is the fitness advantage.
This is the core measurement of the field. And it has a blind spot.
Sequencing a whole population reveals a mutation only once it is common, about 1% or more.
lines.say: Sequencing a whole population reveals a mutation only once it is common, about one percent or more.

lines.t: But every beneficial mutation starts as a single cell, and most of the story happens long before that.
Thousands arise. Most are lost to chance. Others are outcompeted by fitter neighbours, which is called clonal interference.
So the standard approach shows us the winners, but not the race: not how many contenders there were, or how good they were.
To see the race, we would need to follow every lineage from its very first cell.
In 2015, Levy and colleagues flipped the problem. Instead of following mutations, which we cannot predict, follow lineages, which we can label in advance.
lines.say: In twenty fifteen, Levy and colleagues flipped the problem. Instead of following mutations, which we cannot predict, follow lineages, which we can label in advance.

lines.t: Before evolution starts, every cell receives a DNA barcode: a short random sequence, about twenty letters long.
When a lineage gains a beneficial mutation, its barcode becomes more common. We detect the mutation by its effect, without knowing what it is.
Each property of the barcode has a reason. Random, so half a million lineages each get a unique tag: there are over a trillion possible sequences.
Neutral, so the tag itself never changes fitness. Stable and inherited, so every descendant carries it.
And always at the same spot, between fixed sequences, so one PCR reaction can read them all at once.
lines.say: And always at the same spot, between fixed sequences, so one P C R reaction can read them all at once.

lines.t: Putting half a million barcodes into the same spot of the genome takes efficient and precise DNA surgery.
So a landing pad was built into chromosome II, carrying the Cre recombinase gene behind a galactose switch, and half of the URA3 gene.
lines.say: So a landing pad was built into chromosome two, carrying the Cree recombinase gene behind a galactose switch, and half of the U R A 3 gene.

lines.t: A plasmid library carries the barcodes, each beside the other half of URA3. Cre stitches a plasmid into the landing pad at matching lox sites.
lines.say: A plasmid library carries the barcodes, each beside the other half of U R A 3. Cree stitches a plasmid into the landing pad at matching lox sites.

lines.t: Why split URA3? Only a correct integration rebuilds a working gene, so only correctly barcoded cells can grow without uracil. Selection does the quality control.
lines.say: Why split U R A 3? Only a correct integration rebuilds a working gene, so only correctly barcoded cells can grow without uracil. Selection does the quality control.

lines.t: Why the galactose switch? Cre acts only when we want it to. And the leftover lox site is doubly crippled, so the integration is one-way and the barcode stays put.
lines.say: Why the galactose switch? Cree acts only when we want it to. And the leftover lox site is doubly crippled, so the integration is one-way and the barcode stays put.

lines.t: Two replicate populations of about half a million lineages were then evolved by serial transfer for about 168 generations.
lines.say: Two replicate populations of about half a million lineages were then evolved by serial transfer for about one hundred sixty-eight generations.

lines.t: At each transfer, DNA is extracted from millions of frozen cells, so that every lineage is fairly represented, and the barcode region is amplified by PCR.
lines.say: At each transfer, DNA is extracted from millions of frozen cells, so that every lineage is fairly represented, and the barcode region is amplified by P C R.

lines.t: PCR copies some molecules more than others. So each molecule is first tagged with a random identifier, a UMI, and copies sharing a UMI are counted once.
lines.say: P C R copies some molecules more than others. So each molecule is first tagged with a random identifier, a U M I, and copies sharing a U M I are counted once.

lines.t: Index sequences label each sample, so many time points share one sequencing run. Reads per barcode give each lineage's frequency.
Even neutral lineages wobble, through drift and sampling. Measuring that noise is what lets real selection be told apart from luck.
The trajectories tell the story. Neutral lineages slowly sink as the population improves. Lineages carrying beneficial mutations bend upward.
From each curve's shape, the authors inferred how strong the mutation is and when it arose.
In one replicate, about 25,000 lineages carried beneficial mutations. Those worth more than 5% arose at about one per million cells per generation.
lines.say: In one replicate, about twenty-five thousand lineages carried beneficial mutations. Those worth more than five percent arose at about one per million cells per generation.

lines.t: Most benefits were small, and many mutations were already present before the experiment began.
Bulk sequencing would have seen about fifteen. The barcodes turned one history into a measurement of the whole range of possibilities.
The barcodes stay useful after evolution ends. Adaptive clones, still tagged, can be pooled and measured all at once.
In 2020, Kinsler, Geiler-Samerotte and Petrov competed hundreds of them together, against the ancestor at 90% of the flask.
lines.say: In twenty twenty, Kinsler, Geiler-Samerotte and Petrov competed hundreds of them together, against the ancestor at ninety percent of the flask.

lines.t: Why 90%? Each mutant then races the ancestor rather than the other mutants, and the average fitness of the flask barely moves.
lines.say: Why ninety percent? Each mutant then races the ancestor rather than the other mutants, and the average fitness of the flask barely moves.

lines.t: Why cut the ancestor's barcode with a restriction enzyme? Otherwise nine reads in ten would be spent on the ancestor.
And neutral barcoded lineages show how the mean fitness drifts, so that every mutant's slope can be corrected.
One number says how fit a mutant is, but not why. So they measured 292 mutants in 45 environments.
lines.say: One number says how fit a mutant is, but not why. So they measured two hundred ninety-two mutants in forty-five environments.

lines.t: Some were subtle nudges, judged against the variation between repeats of the original condition. Others were strong: salt, drugs, longer transfers.
A mutant's fitness across environments is a fingerprint of its phenotype. Mutants that respond alike probably change similar traits.
Near home, the fingerprints reduce to eight hidden traits, and the first explains 95% of the variation.
lines.say: Near home, the fingerprints reduce to eight hidden traits, and the first explains ninety-five percent of the variation.

lines.t: But traits that barely mattered at home mattered a lot far away. In high salt, mutants that looked alike behaved very differently.
Adaptive mutations, the authors conclude, are locally modular but globally pleiotropic: simple where they evolved, complex elsewhere.
Look back at the chain of reasoning. One clone, so change means mutation. A defined medium, so we know the challenge. Large transfers, so selection beats chance.
Frozen samples and replicates, so history can be compared and repeated. Competition, so fitness means what selection means.
And barcodes, so the whole race becomes countable, not just the winners.
Twenty random letters of DNA, copied faithfully, let us count evolution as it happens.
